<meta>continues from previous page: ...fleeing from flame and abhorring it, such as all salts. We see indeed that, if they are cast into the fire, the aqueous spirit bursts forth with a crackling sound before the flame is conceived. This also happens gently in leaves that are a little more stubborn, the aqueous part breaking out before the oily part conceives flame. But this is perceived most of all in quicksilver, which is not poorly called mineral water. For this, without inflammation, through eruption and simple expansion, almost equals the power of gunpowder; which, when mixed with gunpowder, is also said to multiply its power.</meta>

Similarly, let the <term>Nature Inquired</term> be the transitory nature of flame and its momentary extinction. For the nature of flame does not seem to be fixed and consistent here among us, but rather to be generated at almost every moment, and extinguished immediately. For it is manifest that, in flames which are continued and endure here, that duration is not of the same flame in the <term>individual</term> <gloss>the specific, unique instance</gloss>, but occurs through the succession of new flame generated in order; nor, by any means, does the same flame remain in number. This is easily perceived from the fact that, when the food or fuel of the flame is removed, the flame perishes immediately. The <term>bivium</term> <gloss>a crossroads or two-fold path of inquiry</gloss> regarding this nature is as follows. That momentary nature either occurs because the cause which first generated it is remitting itself, as in light, sounds, and what they call violent motions; or because the flame could remain in its own nature here among us, but is <unclear>by con</unclear>

<summary>Bacon analyzes the transient nature of flame, arguing that ongoing flames are not single, continuous entities but a rapid succession of newly generated flames that require constant fuel to exist. He poses a dual inquiry into whether this fleeting existence is due to the decay of the generating cause or external interference.</summary>
<keywords>flame, extinction, duration, individual, fuel, bivium, causality, nature of light and motion</keywords>
